body:
Purpose of the Coastal Security Scheme

The Coastal Security Scheme (CSS) is a Ministry of Home Affairs initiative designed to strengthen coastal policing through infrastructure, equipment and related support to coastal states and Union Territories.

Coastal police must be able to function in a distinctive environment involving shorelines, fishing harbours, boats and shallow waters. Conventional land-policing resources alone may not be sufficient. The scheme therefore supported facilities and assets such as coastal police stations, check posts, outposts, boats, vehicles and jetties.

The 2 Main Phases

PhaseImplementation periodMain emphasis
Phase I2005–2011Initial strengthening of coastal police stations, outposts, boats and supporting vehicles.
Phase II2011–2020Further coastal-policing infrastructure and resources, including additional stations and jetties.

Phase II was originally approved for implementation from 1 April 2011 to 31 March 2016 and was subsequently extended to 31 March 2020. Therefore, the historical periods of the 2 phases should not be mistaken for proof that the same scheme phase remained open for new implementation in 2026.

The Mumbai attacks of 26 November 2008 prompted a comprehensive review of coastal security. They occurred during Phase I and helped shape later improvements, including stronger central–state coordination.

Coastal Surveillance and Vessel Identification

Coastal security involves both institutional coordination and reliable information about lawful maritime activity. Important measures include:

  • Coastal surveillance systems: Radar and other monitoring facilities help authorities maintain awareness of maritime activity.
  • Vessel registration: Official records help identify fishing and other vessels.
  • Fishermen identification: Identification measures support legitimate fishing activity and communication with authorities.
  • Information sharing: Marine Police, the Coast Guard, Navy, customs and other agencies share relevant information through established channels.
  • Community awareness: Fishing communities receive guidance about safety, reporting suspicious activity and responding to emergencies.

Surveillance technology cannot replace the need for appropriate legal authority and trained personnel. A radar observation, a police investigation and a rescue operation are different functions even when the same incident requires all 3.

National Academy of Coastal Policing

The National Academy of Coastal Policing (NACP) is situated in Devbhoomi Dwarka district, Gujarat. It provides training and capacity building related to coastal policing.

Its Gujarat location is a useful state-specific fact. Coastal-policing training is relevant not only to Gujarat Police personnel but also to personnel of other participating security and enforcement organizations. The Ministry of Home Affairs confirmed its location and training role in a statement dated 17 December 2024.

Exercises and Drills

Authorities conduct exercises to assess whether different agencies can respond together. Two names are especially useful:

  • Sagar Kavach: A coastal-security exercise involving coordination among maritime, police and other relevant authorities.
  • Sajag: A coastal-security drill conducted by the Indian Coast Guard with participation from coastal-security stakeholders.

These are preparedness activities. They should not be confused with actual military operations, naval commands or government schemes.

What Coastal Residents and Fishermen Should Do

Responsible public participation supports coastal security without transferring enforcement duties to civilians. Vessel operators should comply with applicable registration and identification requirements, follow lawful maritime instructions and make use of official safety communications.

People who encounter a possible emergency should contact the appropriate police, Coast Guard or rescue authorities through established channels. They should avoid approaching suspected criminals, unfamiliar hazardous material or a vessel in a dangerous situation. During cyclones or severe-weather warnings, following official advisories and evacuation directions protects both lives and rescue personnel.

Prelims focus

  • Coastal Security Scheme is associated with the Ministry of Home Affairs.
  • CSS Phase I: 2005–2011; CSS Phase II: 2011–2020.
  • The 26 November 2008 Mumbai attacks led to a comprehensive coastal-security review.
  • National Academy of Coastal Policing: Devbhoomi Dwarka, Gujarat.
  • Sagar Kavach is a coastal-security exercise; Sajag is a coastal-security drill.
  • Trap: A coastal-security scheme funds and strengthens policing arrangements; it is not itself a Coast Guard command.

[Sources: Ministry of Home Affairs, Coastal Security Scheme, Phase I and Phase II descriptions, consulted 16 November 2026; Ministry of Home Affairs, Coastal Security Scheme, Annexure VI, October 2024; Ministry of Home Affairs, Training of Coastal Police, 17 December 2024, PIB release 2085166; Ministry of Home Affairs, Measures Taken for Coastal Security, 11 May 2016. Scheme dates reflect the stated implementation periods, not a claim of continuing Phase II implementation in 2026.]

pictures.alt: Timeline separates coastal-security infrastructure phases from post-2008 coordination improvements and the 2024 statement confirming the policing academy.
pictures.caption: Coastal security evolved through infrastructure development, coordination and training.

title: Coastal Security Scheme, Surveillance and Community Participation

body:
The 3 Military Services

India’s principal military services are the Indian Army, Indian Navy and Indian Air Force. Each service specializes in a different domain, but modern national defence often requires them to work together.

ServicePrincipal domainBasic responsibility
Indian ArmyLandDefence of land borders and military operations on land.
Indian NavySeaMaritime defence, protection of national interests at sea and naval operations.
Indian Air ForceAirAir defence, air operations and support for joint military missions.

These are principal areas of responsibility, not absolute divisions. The Navy uses aircraft, the Army uses aviation assets, and the Air Force supports operations involving the other services. Cooperation across these domains is known as jointness.

Constitutional and Governmental Control

The Constitution places the supreme command of the Defence Forces of the Union in the President of India, with its exercise regulated by law. Under India’s parliamentary system, defence policy and major governmental decisions are made through the constitutionally responsible Union government. The President acts on the aid and advice of the Union Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister. The Ministry of Defence administers defence matters through the applicable governmental framework.

The constitutional title Supreme Commander should not be confused with personally directing every military operation. Civilian political control, professional military advice and service-level command are different aspects of defence administration.

The Chief of the Army Staff, Chief of the Naval Staff and Chief of the Air Staff head their respective services. The Chief of Defence Staff is a separate senior office concerned particularly with tri-service matters and jointness.

Military Forces and Central Armed Police Forces

The distinction between military services and Central Armed Police Forces is particularly important in border-security questions.

  • Indian Army: A military service under the defence framework.
  • Border Security Force: A Central Armed Police Force under the Ministry of Home Affairs, responsible for designated border-security functions.
  • Central Industrial Security Force: A Central Armed Police Force under the Ministry of Home Affairs, responsible for security of designated installations and facilities.
  • Indian Coast Guard: An armed force of the Union under the Ministry of Defence, legally and organizationally distinct from the 3 military services.
  • State Police: State-administered law-enforcement institutions, including coastal or marine police arrangements.

The expression armed force does not automatically mean that an organization is a fourth military service. Its parent ministry, governing law and assigned functions must be considered.

Defence and Assistance to Civil Authorities

The principal role of the military is national defence. Nevertheless, the armed forces may also assist civil authorities during major disasters and emergencies when assistance is requested or authorized through the relevant arrangements. Examples include transporting relief supplies, conducting rescue missions and providing temporary medical services.

Such activities are generally described as Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief (HADR). They do not convert the Army, Navy or Air Force into ordinary police forces.

Prelims focus

  • India has 3 principal military services: Army, Navy and Air Force.
  • The President holds the constitutional supreme command of the Defence Forces.
  • The BSF and CISF are under the Ministry of Home Affairs.
  • The Indian Coast Guard is under the Ministry of Defence but is separate from the Navy.
  • HADR means Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief.
  • Trap: A force’s uniform or its use of armed personnel does not by itself determine whether it is a military service.

[Sources: Constitution of India, Article 53; Ministry of Defence, Functions of Chief of Defence Staff, 3 February 2020, PIB release 1601809; Ministry of Defence, Creation of New Department of Military Affairs, 2020; Indian Coast Guard, History and organizational information, consulted 16 November 2026; Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, Beyond Battlefield: Indian Armed Forces in Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief, 15 February 2026.]

pictures.alt: Army, Navy and Air Force are the 3 military services; Coast Guard is separate, BSF and CISF are CAPFs, and Marine Police is state police.
pictures.caption: India’s military services must be distinguished from the Coast Guard, CAPFs and state police.

title: India’s Armed Forces: Structure, Duties and Civilian Control

body:
Why Jointness Is Necessary

The Army, Navy and Air Force possess different capabilities. In a national defence situation, their activities may need to be coordinated so that decisions, resources and support arrangements work towards a common objective.

Jointness means effective cooperation among the military services in planning, training, operations and supporting activities. It does not necessarily mean that their separate identities disappear.

Jointness can improve communication, reduce unnecessary duplication and make better use of resources. It is useful to distinguish cooperation among separate commands from the creation of a permanent command integrating personnel and resources from more than one service.

Creation of the Chief of Defence Staff

The Government of India approved creation of the office of Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) in December 2019. The new arrangements took effect with the establishment of the office and related administrative changes in 2020.

The CDS is intended to strengthen military advice on matters involving more than one service and promote coordination across the armed forces. The position also supports the long-term objective of greater integration.

Main Functions of the CDS

  • Serves as the Principal Military Adviser to the Defence Minister on tri-service matters.
  • Functions as the Permanent Chairman of the Chiefs of Staff Committee.
  • Heads the Department of Military Affairs (DMA) in the Ministry of Defence and acts as its Secretary.
  • Promotes jointness in training, logistics, communication, support services and other shared military functions.
  • Supports inter-service prioritization and planning of defence requirements.
  • Administers tri-service organizations and supports the development of integrated arrangements.

The 3 Service Chiefs continue to exercise their service-specific responsibilities. The creation of the CDS did not make the CDS the direct commander of the Army, Navy and Air Force Chiefs. The official government explanation at the time of creation expressly distinguished the CDS’s advisory and integration functions from direct military command over the Service Chiefs.

Department of Military Affairs

The Department of Military Affairs is part of the Ministry of Defence. Its responsibilities include matters concerning the armed forces assigned to the department, promoting joint planning and facilitating restructuring for greater integration.

The distinction is important: CDS refers to an office, while DMA refers to a government department. Both are associated with defence reforms, but they are not synonyms.

What Is an Integrated Theatre Command?

An integrated theatre command is a proposed organizational arrangement under which resources from different military services would be brought under a common operational command for a defined geographical theatre or assigned function.

The idea is to improve the coordination of military operations and allow service-specific headquarters to concentrate more fully on activities such as developing, training and maintaining their forces.

Several distinctions matter:

  • Single-service command: Belongs primarily to one military service.
  • Tri-service organization or command: Involves all 3 military services under an existing joint arrangement.
  • Integrated theatre command: Refers to the proposed broader operational reorganization of India’s military commands.

India already has the Andaman and Nicobar Command, established in 2001, as a tri-service geographical command. The existence of this command does not mean that all proposed integrated theatre commands have been created.

Legal Reform: Inter-Services Organisations Act

The Inter-Services Organisations (Command, Control and Discipline) Act, 2023 received presidential assent on 15 August 2023 and came into force on 10 May 2024. Its implementing rules came into effect on 27 May 2025.

The Act enables commanders of designated inter-services organizations to exercise the specified command, disciplinary and administrative powers over personnel from different services serving in those organizations, without changing their separate service conditions.

This measure supports joint administration. It does not itself establish an integrated theatre command.

Status of Theatre-Command Reform at the Content Cutoff

A Parliamentary Standing Committee on Defence report for 2026–2027 described continuing discussions about the reorganization of the armed forces into integrated theatre commands. On 23 October 2026, the Defence Secretary publicly stated that a blueprint had been prepared and was awaiting approval at the highest level.

Accordingly, at the 16 November 2026 content cutoff, the proposed new integrated theatre-command structure should be treated as under consideration rather than as an officially operational nationwide command system. Reported numbers and possible headquarters of proposed commands should not be presented as finalized facts.

Prelims focus

  • CDS office approved: December 2019; associated reforms implemented from 2020.
  • CDS heads the Department of Military Affairs and advises on tri-service matters.
  • Andaman and Nicobar Command is an existing tri-service geographical command, established in 2001.
  • Inter-Services Organisations Act: 2023; effective from 10 May 2024.
  • As of 16 November 2026, the proposed new integrated theatre-command structure was awaiting final approval.
  • Trap: A tri-service exercise or the 2023 Act does not mean that a proposed theatre command has become operational.

[Sources: Ministry of Defence, Creation of New Department of Military Affairs, 2020, PIB release 1597425; Ministry of Defence, Functions of Chief of Defence Staff, 3 February 2020, PIB release 1601809; Ministry of Defence, Inter-Services Organisations (Command, Control and Discipline) Act Notified, 10 May 2024, PIB release 2020222; Ministry of Defence, Notification of Rules under the Inter-Services Organisations Act, 28 May 2025, PIB release 2131856; Lok Sabha Standing Committee on Defence, 19th Report, Demands for Grants 2026–2027, section 1.39; Business Standard, Political Leadership Clear on Theatre Commands, Says Defence Secretary, 23 October 2026. Reform status cutoff: 16 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A dated timeline separates completed jointness reforms from continuing theatre-command proposals, not officially operational on 16 November 2026.
pictures.caption: Important reform milestones must be separated from proposals awaiting approval.

title: Chief of Defence Staff, Jointness and Integrated Theatre Commands
